title_zh: 朋友获取率（Friend Acquisition Rate）｜Matt Levine 与代班主持 Mary Childs
subtitle_zh: Kalshi 让 Matt 八点半就上床；再聊 Weil Gotshal 律所挤兑与朝鲜黑客掏空 Binance。
summary_zh: 本期 Money Stuff 由 Matt Levine 与代班主持、《Mary in America》主持人 Mary Childs 对谈。开场 Matt 自嘲中期选举之夜八点半就上床睡了，功劳归于 Kalshi：这家预测市场直接把'谁赢了'告诉他，让他不必再盯 Twitter 上层出不穷的'风向标'与民调聚合。他复盘自己每二十分钟刷一次 Kalshi 的体验——'民主党控制参议院'合约从五点的约 73% 一路涨到 98%，到 98% 他就安心去睡；两人由此讨论押注近乎确定结果的'买债'（bonding）式交易，以及 Matt 对'用选举来对冲'一贯的怀疑（呼应他前几期与 SIG 的 Jeremy Maletz 的对谈）。节目还谈到《New Yorker》一篇关于半导体供应链的报道，捕捉到支撑 AI 的芯片背后何等复杂的人际协作与制造流程，'走进 TSMC 晶圆厂打个喷嚏'都可能扰动全局。此外还聊到 Weil Gotshal 律所的合伙人'挤兑'与那条源于'体面合伙、干一辈子'年代的禁止挖角规则，在如今高度商业化、雇佣兵式的法律行业里已不再适用；以及朝鲜黑客掏空 Binance 一案——洗钱付出约 15% 的高昂成本，去中心化交易所上的对手方却赚了大钱，还笑称'朝鲜付全额费用、五星好评'。

Yeah, we were recording this on Wednesday shortly after I sent out a money stuff saying that my bedtime last night, Tuesday night, election night, was 8.30. But my bedtime most nights is 8.30. Like, that's my target bedtime.

turns.zh: 我说自己常年 8 点半睡觉，多少有点开玩笑的成分，但也只是一点点。那差不多就是我的目标。

I'm like, oh my God, you guys, I found this influencer. It's actually the bullet. And I'm like texting into the ether because my whole group chat's asleep.

turns.zh: 然后还有一个夜班，只有你一个人在上。

turns.zh: 是啊，那个班我一个人守着。

turns.en: And then, like, I wake up at four in the morning and, like, reply to you.
turns.zh: 然后我凌晨四点醒来，回你消息。

turns.en: Okay, three and a half hours. No, that's true.

Because I feel like a lot of people in my world... Stay up late watching midterm elections. Yeah, like, do something for midterm elections. Again, we were recording this on Wednesday, so when I say last night, I mean election night. But you were reading a good book. What was the good book?
turns.zh: 对对。你昨晚几点睡的？11 点半。哦。对……来说这算挺早的了。我在看完一本很好的书。哦，不错不错不错不错不错。因为我觉得我圈子里的很多人……都会熬夜看中期选举。是啊，总之会为中期选举干点什么。再说一次，我们这期是周三录的，所以我说的「昨晚」指的是选举之夜。但你当时在看一本好书。是哪本好书？

turns.en: It was called A Splintering by Dur Aziz Amna. And it's pretty great. I just couldn't stop reading it. And I just had to finish it. Reading can be dangerous like that.
turns.zh: 书名叫 A Splintering，作者是 Dur Aziz Amna。真的很好看，我完全停不下来，非得一口气看完才行。读书有时候就是这么危险。

turns.en: Yeah, I love that experience. Especially when.
turns.zh: 是啊，我太爱那种体验了。尤其是当……

turns.en: It causes you to stay up till 8.45.
turns.zh: 它害你熬到 8 点 45 才睡。

turns.en: There's an election going on? Yeah, I love the experience of reading a novel that is off the news while news is happening. Wait, we should probably say... Hello and welcome to the Money Stuff Podcast. your weekly podcast where we talk about stuff related to money. I'm Matt Levine, and I wrote the Money Stuff column for Bloomberg Opinion.
turns.zh: 外面正在选举的时候？对，我特别喜欢那种体验：在新闻正在发生的时候，读一本跟新闻完全无关的小说。等等，我们大概应该先说……大家好，欢迎收听 Money Stuff 播客，这是我们的每周节目，聊跟钱有关的各种事。我是 Matt Levine，为 Bloomberg Opinion 撰写 Money Stuff 专栏。

turns.en: And I'm Mary Childs. I'm the host of the new podcast, Mary in America, which you can get wherever you get your podcasts.
turns.zh: 我是 Mary Childs。我是新播客 Mary in America 的主持人，你在任何听播客的地方都能听到它。

turns.en: There, we've satisfied our obligations. So I went to bed at 8.30 last night. You were up reading a good book. And I don't want to speak for you, but the people who... I have to thank for my early bedtime last night are Tarek Mansour and the good people at Kalshi, who just told me who won the midterm election so I could not do anything else. But like Kalshi, and I wrote this on Wednesday, provided a great service, which was allowing me to go to bed early because they just told you the answer. In my adult life, there's this long tradition of every two years, there's a midterm election and like there's increasing amounts of like punditry and predictions and like needles and poll aggregators and Twitter and like people on Twitter being like, here are the bellwether things to look for.
turns.zh: 好了，义务履行完毕。所以说，我昨晚 8 点半就睡了，你则熬着看完了一本好书。我不想替你说，但我昨晚能早睡，要感谢的人是 Tarek Mansour 和 Kalshi 那帮好人——他们直接告诉我中期选举谁赢了，这样我就可以什么别的都不干。Kalshi，我周三就把这段写下来了，提供了一项伟大的服务：让我能早点睡，因为他们直接把答案告诉你了。在我成年以后的人生里，有个由来已久的传统：每两年就有一次中期选举，然后各种评论、预测、指针（needle）、民调聚合网站、Twitter，以及 Twitter 上那些人说「这些才是你该盯的风向标（bellwether）」，数量越来越多。

turns.en: And like, I've seen enough people publishing posts.
turns.zh: 而且我见过太多人发帖，

turns.en: That are like, here are the 25 things to look at to tell you who's going to have a good night. And like, here are the 10 things not to look at because they're misleading. And then like you go on Twitter and it's like some other guys like, no, this is the real thing to look at. And you're like, I don't know who this guy is, but like maybe he's the savant who knows everything. Right. And like, there's this proliferation of like, possible information that three hours ahead of the actual election call gives you like information or what you think is information or just like a, you know, dead end rabbit hole about who's going to win the election. And you're like, ah, who's going to win the election. And there are obviously people who are like, we will solve this problem by just telling you the answer. Like Nate Silver is good at that. But like, if you are like a professional, uh, forecaster held to the standards of a journalist organization. Like you have to do that in a somewhat cautious way. And then Cal, she's like, we'll just tell you the answer. We'll just tell you the answer as fast as we can get it. And we will have people who are in charge of like looking at Twitter and looking at the guy who's like, oh, this is the bellwether and evaluating that guy's credibility and putting that into a like Bayesian model that updates like the rest of the people on Twitter shouting and And we'll just like reduce all of that down to one probability number. And then like, you know, like what I did last night or like yesterday at like five o'clock is I just put up calci on my laptop and like every 20 minutes I'd look. I think the Democrat controlled Senate started at like, I don't know, 73% at around five o'clock. And, you know, it ticked up to like 80%. And I was like, okay, that means that like there's a four out of five chance that the next tick will be up, kind of. And then, um, they went up to like 88, it went down again. I was like, Hmm. Hmm. And then it like went up to 95 by like seven 30 or something. And I was like, I have seen enough. And I went to bed. I mean, I went to bed at eight 30 when it was like 98%. And like, I guess this has happened before, but like the combination of prediction markets being so much bigger now, so much more mainstream, like they have partnerships with news organizations. It just like made the information environment so much cleaner and nicer and more user friendly and more relaxing. And I have said on this podcast, some things that might be taken as unkind to Kalshi and I hereby retract all of them. I don't really, I don't really, I don't retract all of them. Like I stand by everything I've said about like sports gambling, but Kalshi is sponsoring all these news organizations now. And I'm like, I can sponsor many stuff, but it's fine. I love it. I love it. I love it. And this is what I wrote. I would say, it's such a strange business because every two years, they're hugely socially useful. And it's like, great job, guys. And then the other 729 days, it's like, sports gambling. I don't know. Yeah.
turns.zh: 帖子内容是「这 25 个指标能告诉你今晚谁会风光」。又或者「这 10 个别看，因为它们会误导你」。然后你上 Twitter，又有人说：不对，这个才是真正该看的。你会想：我不知道这人是谁，但说不定他就是那个无所不知的天才。对吧。于是就出现了大量这类「可能的信息」——在官方正式宣布结果的三小时之前，给你信息、或者你以为的信息，或者干脆是一条死胡同式的兔子洞，告诉你谁会赢下选举。你就在那儿想：啊，到底谁会赢。当然也有人会说：我们直接告诉你答案，就把这个问题解决了。比如 Nate Silver 就很擅长这个。但如果你是那种受新闻机构标准约束的专业预测人士，你就得用相当谨慎的方式来做这件事。而 Kalshi 的态度是：我们就直接告诉你答案，能多快拿到就多快告诉你。而且我们会有专人负责盯 Twitter、盯那个说「哦，这是风向标」的人，评估这人的可信度，把它放进一个贝叶斯（Bayesian）模型里，跟着 Twitter 上其他人的叫喊一起更新，最后把所有这一切压缩成一个概率数字。然后，你知道我昨晚、或者说昨天下午五点左右干了什么吗？我就在笔记本上打开 Kalshi，每 20 分钟看一次。我记得「民主党控制参议院」这个合约在五点左右大概是 73% 起步吧。然后它慢慢涨到 80% 左右。我就想：好，那意味着下一次跳动有四五成的概率是往上，差不多这个意思。然后又涨到 88 左右，接着又跌回去了。我就想：嗯……嗯。然后到了大概 7 点半左右涨到 95%。我就想：我看够了。于是我去睡觉了。我是说，我在 98% 左右的时候、8 点半上床。我觉得这种事以前也发生过，但预测市场现在规模大得多、主流得多，还跟新闻机构有合作关系，这就让整个信息环境变得干净得多、舒服得多、好用得多、令人放松得多。我在这个播客上说过一些可能会被解读为对 Kalshi 不友好的话，我在此全部收回。我不，我不，我并不全部收回。关于体育博彩我说过的话我全都坚持。但 Kalshi 现在赞助了这么多新闻机构，我就想：他们也可以来赞助 Money Stuff 嘛，不过这没什么。我喜欢，我喜欢，我太喜欢了。我周三写的是这么一句：我会说，这是一门很奇怪的生意，因为每两年有一次，他们的社会价值巨大，你会想说「干得漂亮，伙计们」；而另外那 729 天，它就是体育博彩。我也不知道。是啊。

turns.en: Well, it's nice because this is what it was born to do. It's totally what it was born to do. It was born out of Brexit. And it really works for what it was meant to work for. What else can it work for? I don't know. Other things. Sports gambling.
turns.zh: 这挺好的，因为这正是它天生该做的事。完全是它天生该做的事。它是从 Brexit 里诞生的，而且它在它本该发挥作用的场景里确实管用。那它还能用在什么别的地方？我不知道。别的玩意儿。体育博彩。

turns.en: Yeah. Right. There is, like, an obvious connection between betting on elections and betting on sports. And, you know, of course, they're like, well, the next thing is betting on sports. And there's, like, an interesting history there where, like, back in the Biden CFTC, they were trying to stop Cal State from doing election bets. And the CFTC was like, this is, like, gaming. And Cal State's like, this isn't gaming. Sports betting would be gaming. We wouldn't do sports betting. We just want to do election betting, right? And then, like, the Trump CFTC comes in and it's like, wow, sports betting, obviously. There's an obvious extension from this to sports betting. But, like, At no point am I going to be watching the Super Bowl and pulling up Kalshi to be like, I don't know who's going to win. Let's find out on Kalshi. I'm going to watch the game.
turns.zh: 对，没错。赌选举和赌体育之间显然有关联。而且，你知道，当然，他们的说法是：那下一步就是体育博彩。这里有段挺有意思的历史：Biden 时期的 CFTC 曾经想阻止 Kalshi 做选举赌盘。CFTC 说这属于博彩（gaming）。Kalshi 说这不是博彩，体育博彩才是博彩，我们不会做体育博彩，我们只想做选举赌盘，对吧？然后 Trump 时期的 CFTC 上任了，态度是：哇，体育博彩，那当然，从这事延伸到体育博彩是明摆着的。但问题是，我绝对不会在看 Super Bowl 的时候掏出 Kalshi 说「我不知道谁会赢，我们去 Kalshi 上看看」。我要看比赛。

turns.en: But that's a nice point because the texture is so different. I don't derive any joy from the mechanics of vote counting.
turns.zh: 但这是个很好的点，因为两者的质感完全不同。我从计票这种机械过程里得不到任何乐趣。

turns.en: Right. And some people do.
turns.zh: 对。但有些人能。

turns.en: The mechanics of winning is the point of sport.
turns.zh: 获胜过程本身的机制才是体育的重点。

turns.en: Right, right, right, right.
turns.zh: 对对对对。

turns.en: Only sick people do.
turns.zh: 只有变态才干得出来。

turns.en: Right. No, I agree. Sick people do. But no, I agree. The watching of election results is, I think, for almost everybody, extremely unpleasant. but you do want to know the answer. Whereas like the watching of sports results is the whole point of sports. And also like, I'm not a normal sports fan in this way, but like I like to watch sports and like my life won't be ruined if my team loses, you know, like I don't care that much about the result. I want to watch the game. Like elections are the exact opposite. Like I would rather be like knocked out and wake up the next day knowing the answer rather than watch it. And Kalshi provides that service. It's great.
turns.zh: 对。不，我同意。变态才干得出来。不过是的，我同意。看选举结果这件事，我觉得对几乎所有人来说都极其难受，但你确实想知道答案。而看体育比赛的结果，那才是体育的全部意义。另外，在这一点上我不是个正常的体育迷：我喜欢看比赛，但如果我支持的队输了，我的人生不会被毁掉，你知道吧，我对结果没那么在意，我想看的是比赛本身。选举正好相反。我宁愿被人一棍子打晕，第二天醒来直接知道答案，也不想盯着看。而 Kalshi 提供的就是这项服务。太棒了。

turns.en: Okay, so you said that it's socially useful, and I understand the social utility of your bedtime.
turns.zh: 好，那你说它有社会价值，我也理解它对你睡觉时间的社会价值。

turns.en: Yeah, I don't know that I have a strong argument that it's, like, broadly socially useful, but go on.
turns.zh: 是啊，我也说不清自己有没有强有力的论据来证明它在更广泛的意义上有社会价值，不过你继续说。

turns.en: That's my question, is, like, so how else is it? Like, my friend Natalie Fratto just interviewed Tarek about Kalshi, and she had him basically explain, like, okay, if I'm an ice cream salesperson, how can I use Kalshi to, like, offset my risks?
turns.zh: 这就是我的问题：那它还能怎么有用？比如我朋友 Natalie Fratto 刚采访了 Tarek，聊 Kalshi，她基本上让他解释：好吧，如果我是个卖冰淇淋的，我要怎么用 Kalshi 来对冲（hedge）我的风险？

turns.en: I'm making a series of horrible hand gestures here, but sure, go on.
turns.zh: 我在这儿做一连串很难看的手势，不过行，你继续。

turns.en: Yeah, it was not vulgar, we should be clear.
turns.zh: 是啊，我们得说清楚，那些手势并不下流。

turns.en: I was about to do vulgar hand motions and then I decided to not do them. Wow.
turns.zh: 我本来要做下流手势的，后来决定不做了。哇。

turns.en: Thank you. Such restraint.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，真是克制。

turns.en: Ice cream hedging. Sorry. Yeah.
turns.zh: 冰淇淋对冲。抱歉。是啊。

turns.en: The ice cream hedging. I don't know. I struggle to find like sometimes, okay. Hedging Brexit risk. I get what difference does it make to know that results of the election four hours different other than your bedtime? I don't know.
turns.zh: 冰淇淋对冲。我不知道。有时候我确实很难想到——好吧，对冲 Brexit 风险，这个我懂。提前四小时知道选举结果，除了你的睡觉时间，还能带来什么区别？我不知道。

turns.en: Okay. So a couple of points on that. I agree that the four hours thing, one, it's intensely useful for me. And two, it's really good. It's like accurate. When Kelshi is like, At, you know, 8.30, like, there's a 98% chance of the Democrats winning. Like, that's fairly definitive. It's 98% definitive. Whereas, like, when Kelshi, two days out, is like, oh, there's a 73% chance of Democrats winning. It's like, you know, that.
turns.zh: 好。关于这个我有几点。第一，四小时提前量这件事，我同意——它对我极其有用；第二，它真的很准。当 Kalshi 在 8 点半左右说民主党有 98% 的概率获胜时，那基本上就是定局了，是 98% 的定局。而当 Kalshi 在还剩两天的时候说「哦，民主党有 73% 的概率获胜」，那就是，你知道，那种程度。

turns.en: Not useful, yeah.
turns.zh: 没那么有用，是啊。

turns.en: It's useful, but it's like, you know, it's much less useful. But no, I agree that, like, four hours, there's no, like, economic impact to that, right? I do think that, like, you know, a month out, Kelshi will give you odds that are pretty good. Like, their research suggests that.
turns.zh: 它有用，但你知道，用处小得多。不过是的，我同意：提前四小时，这没什么经济影响，对吧？我确实认为，在还剩一个月的时候，Kalshi 给出的赔率是相当不错的，他们自己的研究就是这么显示的。

turns.en: A wide bid ask, yeah.
turns.zh: 买卖价差（bid ask）很宽，是啊。

turns.en: Yeah. It's not that wide. And their research suggests that their markets are pretty well calibrated.
turns.zh: 是啊，其实没宽到那种程度。而且他们的研究显示，他们的市场校准得相当好。

And everyone quoted his paper about this because he wrote a paper like five years ago about runs on law firms. And what he says is like law firms that collapse, you know, unsurprisingly, usually have some financial distress, but people are surprised at how mild the distress is. And like while like, I don't know what distress means, but like they were quite profitable companies. partners made an average of, I don't know, five or so million dollars a year last year. Like they were, you know, the top 30 in revenue. Like they're a great business. But what happened is that there are better businesses that could pick off the best, you know, the most lucrative wild partners, right? Like, so there are very lucrative businesses and law firms. And, you know, classically these days, everyone says the lucrative business is private equity, which I think means some amount of private equity M & A and some amount of fund formation. And it's stuff that is high dollar, high volume. You can do with lots of associates where like a partner is bringing in a lot of business and farming it out to a lot of like lower level people. And those firms can go to the most lucrative partners at a place like Weill Gottschall and be like, well, double your salary. And those people leave. And they take the most lucrative business with them. And then the average partner profit at Weill goes down And it cascades where while it can't pay its people enough to keep them from going elsewhere, and then eventually there's nobody left.
turns.zh: 现在对律所来说是个很奇怪的时代，对吧？因为我写过这个。大家对律所、投行、对冲基金等等常用的那句话——对冲基金不太适用，但也有点适用——是：资产每天傍晚坐电梯下楼，对吧？这对对冲基金不成立，但你知道，资产是在对冲基金里面的。总之，这有点跑题了。但 Weil 这件事的关键是……我引用了 John Morley 的一篇论文，他其实是我在法学院时同期的人。他是 Yale 的法学教授，研究律所经济学。所有人都在引用他这篇论文，因为他大概五年前写过一篇关于律所挤兑的文章。他说的是：倒闭的律所，不出意外，通常都有些财务困境，但大家惊讶的是这个困境有多轻微。而 Weil——我不知道「困境」该怎么定义——但他们是一家非常赚钱的公司。合伙人去年平均一年赚大概五百万美元左右。他们的营收排在前三十。这是门很好的生意。但发生的情况是：有更好的生意平台可以把最赚钱的那批 Weil 合伙人一个个挖走，对吧？律所里有些业务非常赚钱。如今大家通常说最赚钱的业务是私募股权（private equity），我想这包括一部分私募股权 M&A 和一部分基金设立（fund formation）。这类业务金额高、量大，可以用很多 Associate 来做——合伙人拉来大量业务，然后分派给很多初级的人去做，这样计费小时数就能很多，非常非常赚钱。有些律所拥有很大的平台来做这件事。这些律所就可以去找 Weil Gotshal 那边最赚钱的合伙人说：我们把你的薪水翻倍。于是这些人就走了，还把最赚钱的业务带走了。接着 Weil 的平均合伙人利润就下降，然后层层传导：Weil 付不出足够的钱来留住人，最后就一个人都剩不下了。

turns.en: An un-network effect, yeah.
turns.zh: 一种反向的网络效应，是啊。

turns.en: Yeah. And I mean, one thing that is strange about this is that you could imagine roughly similar dynamics at an investment bank, right? Where like some manager directors are more lucrative than others and they could all leave to more lucrative platforms and then the thing would collapse. And investment banks know this and So they have non-competes and they have gardening leave and they have stock that vests over time so that people have some incentive to be locked in and there's a real cost to them of switching. Whereas in law firms, it's kind of like, you know, if a new firm will pay you $ 100, 000 more than your old firm, you go in part because like a little bit more money is worth it. And in part because like that firm is really more stable. And law firms can't have non-competes and they actually like partners have equity issues.
turns.zh: 是啊。我是说，这件事奇怪的一点是：你完全可以想象投行里出现差不多的动态，对吧？比如有些董事总经理（managing director）比其他人更赚钱，他们全都可以跳槽去更赚钱的平台，然后那家投行就崩了。投行清楚这一点，所以他们有竞业禁止条款（non-compete）、有花园休假（gardening leave）、有分期归属的股票，这样人们就有被锁定的动机，跳槽对他们来说有实实在在的成本。而在律所，情况就有点像：如果新律所愿意比老律所多付你十万美元，你就会走——一部分原因是多这点钱值得，另一部分原因是那家律所确实更稳定。而律所不能有竞业禁止条款，而且实际上合伙人还有股权问题。

turns.en: Look down on them.

turns.en: You're right. They can't have them, but they also like partners have equity in the firm, but they can't be like, oh, we lock up your equity for a long time. They have to like be sort of reasonable about returning your equity to you. And the reason for that is like rules of legal ethics, which say basically that you're not allowed, you know, lawyers are not allowed to prevent other lawyers from practicing law, which like in a world where like lawyers are like doctors and there's a shortage of lawyers and like everyone needs legal services. turns.zh: 你说得对。他们不能有竞业禁止，而且合伙人虽然在律所里有股权，但律所不能说「哦，我们把你的股权锁定很长时间」。他们必须相当合理地把你的股权退还给你。原因在于法律职业伦理规则，它基本上是说：律师不允许阻止其他律师执业。在一个律师像医生一样、存在律师短缺、人人都需要法律服务的世界里，确保法律服务得到公平供给非常重要，所以这条规则是说得通的，对吧？

turns.zh: 并不短缺。而且我们现在没那么绅士了。我们不像以前那样讲究绅士风度了。

turns.en: Which, like, one aspect of working at a multi-strat hedge fund is, like, you have some years of $ 20 million compensation, and then you have some years of gardening leave. At a law firm, you don't. I mean, you have some years of your firm collapses, but hopefully you're on the right side of that. So I do think that, like, the collapse of Weill is, like, probably about, like, some particular partners leaving for particular firms for particular reasons, but, like, people see it in the shadow of a general transition in, like, law firm economics, which is partly... like the rise of these big firms that have like very lucrative economics and that optimize for doing like very lucrative private equity work. And partly about like, nobody knows what's coming in AI in legal services. One possibility is something like what everyone always says about all of these, you know, financial services firms, which is that, you know, the big lucrative partners with the big lucrative relationships can continue to exploit those big lucrative relationships and to do much more work with many fewer associates because AI will do all the work for them and they'll just bring in the business. And so you will have partners making $ 50 million a year and no associates being trained behind them. And that's one possible model. And like that model would, I think, be very good for the giant platforms that have, you know already optimized for this environment and very bad for places like while that are a little bit behind and then there are other possible models like clients will just type their legal questions into ai and the ai will answer them and they will never call a law firm and the lucrative partners will wait by the phone for the phone to ring So I don't know, but like AI is very much unsettling law firms and like the wild collapse is probably not an AI story, but it's like, it feels like part of that unsettlement.
turns.zh: 在一家多策略对冲基金（multi-strat hedge fund）工作有一个特点：你有几年拿两千万美元的薪酬，然后你有几年在花园休假。在律所就没有这种安排。我是说，你有几年是律所倒闭了，但希望你站在对的那一边。所以我确实觉得，Weil 的倒闭大概是因为某些特定合伙人出于某些特定原因跳去了某些特定律所，但人们是在律所经济学整体转型的阴影下看待它的。这个转型一部分是……那些拥有非常赚钱的经济模型、专门为高利润私募股权业务做优化的大所的崛起；另一部分是，没人知道 AI 会给法律服务带来什么。一种可能性，就是大家对所有这类金融服务公司总会说的那种：手握大额赚钱客户关系的大合伙人可以继续变现这些关系，用少得多的 Associate 完成多得多的工作，因为 AI 会替他们干活，他们只管把业务拉进来。于是你会有年入五千万美元的合伙人，而他们身后没有正在培养的 Associate。这是一种可能的模型。我认为这种模型对那些已经为这个环境做过优化的巨型平台非常有利，而对像 Weil 这样稍微落后一点的地方非常不利。然后还有其他可能的模型：客户直接把法律问题打给 AI，AI 回答他们，他们永远不会打电话给律所，而那些赚钱的合伙人就守着电话等它响。所以我也不知道，但 AI 确实在极大地搅动律所行业，Weil 的倒闭大概不是一个 AI 故事，但它感觉像是那场搅动的一部分。

turns.en: Like presages. Yeah. It's a mild, a mild amount of AI anxiety resulting in a partner run.
turns.zh: 像是预兆。是啊。这是一种轻微的、轻微的 AI 焦虑，结果引发了一场合伙人大逃亡。

turns.en: It's not X risk, but you know.
turns.zh: 这不是 X-risk，但你知道的。

turns.en: It was turned out for them. If you had not left law, What would that world look like? Are you a 50 million? Are you a private equity? You don't like dinners very much.
turns.zh: 他们最后就落得这样。如果你当年没有离开法律行业，那个世界会是什么样？你是年入五千万那种？还是做私募股权那种？你不太喜欢那些晚宴。

turns.en: It's very interesting. I think the honest answer is if I had not left law, I would have just simply died of overwork. That's being real here. The firm would not have collapsed.
turns.zh: 这个问题很有意思。我觉得诚实的答案是：如果我没有离开法律行业，我就是单纯地过劳死了。我说真的。那家律所并不会因此倒闭。

turns.en: I would have collapsed.
turns.zh: 我会垮掉的。

turns.en: Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah. The firm would have been fine. I left law because I was physically breaking down. Had I survived that, I worked at Wachtell Lifton. I really liked it. I continue to like it. I like the people there. I like its vibe. There is some chance that I would be an M & A lawyer at Wachtell Lifton right now. I don't think I'd be making $ 20 million a year because those people have fairly lockstep compensation. That is the last, I mean, to some extent, and this is an exaggeration, but to some extent, it's the last of the old school partnerships where people get paid by seniority and it's not like, oh, we pay the big rainmakers the most. Because it's the idea is that it's a firm that brings in the business on the strength of the firm. And so we don't need to go out.
turns.zh: 哦，是是是。律所会好好的。我离开法律行业是因为我的身体正在垮掉。如果我挺过来了——我当时在 Wachtell Lipton 工作，我真的很喜欢那里，我至今仍然喜欢。我喜欢那里的人，喜欢那里的氛围。有一定概率我现在会是 Wachtell Lipton 的一名 M&A 律师。我不觉得我会一年赚两千万美元，因为那里的薪酬相当「论资排辈」（lockstep）。那是最后的——我是说，某种程度上，这有夸张成分，但某种程度上，它是最后一批老派合伙制之一：按资历付钱，而不是「哦，我们给最能拉业务的人付最多」。因为它的理念是：这家律所靠整个平台的实力去拉业务，所以我们不需要出去拉业务。

turns.en: Still gentlemaning over there.
turns.zh: 那边还在讲绅士风度。

turns.en: Yeah. Still gentlemaning a little bit. Now this is new things have changed and they've lost partners and no one is immune to this.
turns.zh: 是啊，还有一点绅士范儿。不过现在情况变了，新东西来了，他们也流失了合伙人，没有人能免疫于这件事。

turns.en: So, okay. So you would be like a 20 millioner.
turns.zh: 好吧。所以你会是个两千万富翁。

turns.en: I don't think people at Wachtell make 20 million, but like the average partner profit at Wachtell is something like 10.
turns.zh: 我不觉得 Wachtell 的人能拿到两千万，但 Wachtell 的平均合伙人利润大概是一千万这个量级。

turns.en: Oh, that is interesting, isn't it?
turns.zh: 哦，这挺有意思的，不是吗？

turns.en: Right. So it's real money.
turns.zh: 对。所以那是真金白银。

turns.en: Sorry, Matt. I regret asking.
turns.zh: 抱歉，Matt。我后悔问了。

turns.en: They sued Elon Musk to close the Twitter deal. And after that happened, he sued them for their feedback. And in his complaint, he pointed out that Wachtel's fee for just for like, you know, whatever, you know, a month of suing Elon Musk to close the Twitter deal was something like $ 90 million. It was $ 1 million per partner at Wachtel. So it added $ 1 million to each partner's profit at Wachtel. Just that deal. Anyway, it's a good business. Good business, hard, hard, hard working business. Not, I think, all in all for me, but I liked it a lot. I liked the work and the people and the vibe. I just, I was not physically capable of continuing it. The generation of partners that I like worked with at Wachtel were like people who were committed to Wachtel and never known another place, you know? And I think like the younger generation, sometimes people would leave for, you know, $ 20 million jobs elsewhere. And had I stayed and become a partner there, Would I have left for a $ 20 million job elsewhere? I hope so. I hope this alternative me is getting rich, you know?
turns.zh: 他们起诉 Elon Musk，要求完成 Twitter 那笔交易。在那之后，他反过来起诉了他们，要求退还律师费。在他的诉状里，他指出 Wachtell 光是为了——你知道，反正就是为起诉 Elon Musk 要求交割 Twitter 交易忙活一个月左右——收的律师费大约就是九千万美元。这相当于 Wachtell 每位合伙人一百万美元，也就是说光是这一单就给 Wachtell 每位合伙人的利润增加了一百万美元。总之，这是门好生意。好生意，非常非常辛苦的那种生意。总的来看，我觉得它不适合我，但我很喜欢它。我喜欢那份工作、那些人、那种氛围。我只是身体上撑不下去了。我在 Wachtell 共事的那一代合伙人，都是那种忠于 Wachtell、从没待过别的地方的人，你知道吧？而我觉得年轻一代，有时候会有人为了别处两千万美元的工作离开。如果我一直留下并成为那里的合伙人，我会为了别处一份两千万美元的工作离开吗？我希望会。我希望那个平行版本的我正在发财，你知道吧？

turns.en: He's so rich. He's not well, but he's rich.
turns.zh: 他太有钱了。他身体不好，但他有钱。

turns.en: Not well. But like, this alternative me gave up on health a long time ago. This alternative me is in bad shape. Yeah, yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 身体不好。但是，那个平行版本的我早就放弃健康了。那个我身体状况很糟。是啊是啊是啊。

turns.en: No, he's in an MRI machine right now.
turns.zh: 不，他这会儿正躺在 MRI 机器里。

turns.en: He's maximizing profits while he can. Seriously. I cannot tell you how much my body broke down in a year and a half.
turns.zh: 他在趁还能挣的时候把利润最大化。说真的，我没法告诉你一年半里我的身体垮得有多厉害。

turns.en: Your body rejected it. The mind was willing. Yeah, I'm sorry.
turns.zh: 你的身体拒绝了它。心灵是愿意的。是啊，我很抱歉。

turns.en: Very much so. Very much so.
turns.zh: 非常愿意，非常愿意。

turns.en: Well, you love your job, and you're deeply loyal to Bloomberg, and those things are great.
turns.zh: 嗯，你热爱你的工作，你对 Bloomberg 又极其忠诚，这些都是很棒的事。

turns.en: That's true. And I get $ 20 million a year. It's fabulous.
turns.zh: 没错。而且我一年挣两千万美元。太棒了。

turns.en: Everybody send in your donations. I'm just kidding. I should stop making this kind of joke on the air.
turns.zh: 大家都来捐款吧。我开玩笑的。我不该在节目里开这种玩笑。

turns.en: It's okay. With the Kalshi sponsorship, we're great.
turns.zh: 没关系。有了 Kalshi 的赞助，我们好得很。

turns.en: Yeah, yeah, yeah. We're doing amazing. So last Friday, which I know because I was supposed to have breakfast with a friend of mine who works in crypto land and he could not have breakfast with me because of North Korea, which I found deeply rude. He texts me. He's like, I'm sorry, Pyongyang. Which helped make me feel special when we didn't end up having breakfast. Like it feels nice to blame like North Korea instead of something less important.
turns.zh: 是是是，我们好得不得了。所以上周五——我之所以记得，是因为我本来要跟一个在加密圈工作的朋友吃早餐，而他因为朝鲜没法跟我吃早餐，我觉得这非常无礼。他给我发短信说：抱歉，Pyongyang。这在我们最终没吃成早餐的时候，反倒让我觉得自己挺特别的。把锅甩给朝鲜，比甩给什么不那么重要的东西，感觉要好得多。

turns.en: Canceling on you or anyone for North Korea is a great reason to cancel. I'm going to start using that.
turns.zh: 因为朝鲜而放你或者任何人的鸽子，都是一个绝佳的取消理由。我要开始用这个了。

turns.en: Yeah, it's legitimate.
turns.zh: 是啊，这很正当。

turns.en: I can't make dinner tonight. North Korea.
turns.zh: 今晚的晚饭我来不了了。朝鲜。

turns.en: I don't think it's quite as valid when you if you use that on me, I would not feel happy.
turns.zh: 我觉得如果是你用在我身上，就不那么站得住脚了，我不会高兴的。

turns.en: OK, so your friend canceled on you because of North Korea, because North Korea allegedly. North Korea denied this. Allegedly.
turns.zh: 好吧，所以你朋友因为朝鲜放了你鸽子，因为是朝鲜「据说」干的。朝鲜否认了这件事。据说。

turns.en: They would never do that.
turns.zh: 他们绝不会干那种事。

turns.en: Yeah. Somebody.
turns.zh: 是啊。有人……

turns.en: Hacked.
turns.zh: 黑了……

turns.en: Allegedly North Korea.
turns.zh: 据说是朝鲜。

turns.en: Somebody hacked Binance.
turns.zh: 有人黑了 Binance。

turns.en: Hacked Binance and took $ 6. 3 billion of crypto out of there.
turns.zh: 黑了 Binance，从里面拿走了 63 亿美元的加密货币。

turns.en: As fast as they could.
turns.zh: 以最快的速度。

turns.en: As fast as they could.
turns.zh: 能多快就多快。

turns.en: How'd they do it, Matt?
turns.zh: 他们是怎么做到的，Matt？

turns.en: Allegedly. Well, apparently through like fake job interviews, which is so embarrassing.
turns.zh: 据说。嗯，看起来是通过假的求职面试，这实在太丢人了。

turns.en: Apparently on LinkedIn.
turns.zh: 看起来是在 LinkedIn 上。

turns.en: Apparently.
turns.zh: 看起来是。

turns.en: I made this up, but it says it's like a job searching platform. Is there another one? Glassdoor?
turns.zh: 这是我瞎编的，但它说那是一个求职平台。还有别的吗？Glassdoor？

turns.en: I have no reason to believe that any of this took place in the United States. But I don't know what other platforms there are wherever Binance operates, which is famously nowhere. It's stateless.
turns.zh: 我没有任何理由相信这些事情发生在美国境内。但我不知道在 Binance 运营的那些地方还有什么别的平台——而众所周知，它哪儿都不运营。它是无国界的。

turns.en: There is no domicile.
turns.zh: 它没有注册地。

turns.en: Yeah. No domicile. But yeah, so apparently they like tricked someone through like months of social engineering. They tricked someone into thinking he was interviewing at some other job.
turns.zh: 是啊，没有注册地。不过是的，所以看起来他们通过好几个月的社会工程学（social engineering）骗了某个人，让这个人以为自己是在应聘另一份工作。

turns.en: Just devastating for that person.
turns.zh: 对那个人来说简直是毁灭性的。

turns.en: And they were like, please download this coding assignment. And it was like, surprise, we've taken all.
turns.zh: 然后他们说：请下载这份编程作业。结果就是——惊喜吧，我们已经拿走了……

turns.en: Of Binance's money.
turns.zh: Binance 所有的钱。

turns.en: And I just like.
turns.zh: 我就……

turns.en: You would feel so bad.
turns.zh: 你会难受得要命。

turns.en: It's quite bad to download malware at your work. Quite bad. Right.
turns.zh: 在公司电脑上下载恶意软件是相当糟糕的事。相当糟糕。对吧。

turns.en: You know, they have those training sessions.
turns.zh: 你知道的，公司都有那种培训课。

turns.en: Right. But also it's like, why are you downloading this? I was interviewing for another job. It's like really bad. It's like, you get no like forgiveness for that.
turns.zh: 对。但另一方面也是：你为什么要下载这个？我在面试另一份工作啊。这真的很糟。这种事你得不到任何原谅。

turns.en: Yeah. It would be better if you were a spy.
turns.zh: 是啊。如果你是个间谍反倒还好一点。

turns.en: Yeah. Apparently that's what happened. And, They drained $ 6. 3 billion from Binance. And there are a couple of new things about it. One is that half of the money, give or take, was in, let's say, stablecoins. Maybe some other stuff that has similar characteristics. But centralized stablecoins like Tether and USDC, where the stablecoin issuer... The stablecoin is just a claim. This is like a ledger entry at the stablecoin issuer. And the issuer can be like, no, we're not going to pay out a dollar to the North Korean hackers who stole it. So basically all those tethers and USDCs were canceled, which is on the one hand, very like, oh, that's not crypto. That's not what Satoshi would have wanted.
turns.zh: 是啊。看起来事情就是这样。他们从 Binance 抽走了 63 亿美元。这件事有几个新特点。一是这笔钱里差不多有一半，姑且说，是稳定币（stablecoin），也许还有一些特性类似的东西。但那是像 Tether 和 USDC 这样的中心化稳定币——在稳定币发行方那里……稳定币本质上只是一笔索取权，就是发行方账本上的一条记录。而发行方可以说：不，我们不会向偷走它的朝鲜黑客兑付一美元。所以基本上那些 Tether 和 USDC 全被注销了。这一方面很像是——哦，这不是加密货币，这不是 Satoshi 想要的样子。

turns.en: It's antithetical to the whole thing.
turns.zh: 这跟整套理念是根本对立的。

turns.en: It's so antithetical to the whole thing. On the other hand, it's like, don't be stupid. Like that's how it should work. Like you've stolen money and the banks reversed the transaction. It's like, it's so obviously superior and it's just great. It's just great.
turns.zh: 跟整套理念极其对立。但另一方面，这就像是在说：别犯傻了，本来就该这样运作。你偷了钱，银行把这笔交易撤销了。这明显优越得多，简直太好了。太好了。

turns.en: For it to work this way. Yeah, of course.
turns.zh: 它能这样运作。是啊，当然。

turns.en: Like this is how it should work. They stole the money and like, The bank was like, no, give it back. And then it was fixed. Half of it. The other half was crypto and was not fixed.
turns.zh: 本来就该这样运作。他们偷了钱，然后银行说：不行，还回来。于是就修好了——一半修好了。另一半是加密货币，没能修好。

turns.en: Are you saying that DeFi can't exist?
turns.zh: 你是在说 DeFi 没法存在吗？

turns.en: No. If you're a real purist, you can do stable coins that are vault-based and are not centralized and so can't be canceled.
turns.zh: 不是。如果你是个真正的纯粹主义者，你可以做基于金库（vault）的稳定币，不是中心化的，因此也没法被注销。

turns.en: So much effort.
turns.zh: 太费劲了。

turns.en: A lot of stuff that is DeFi in the sense that it runs on decentralized exchanges is one leg of the trade is USDC or USDT, right? It's like a centralized stable coin. I just think that Binance would be in much worse shape had the North Korean hackers been able to take all of the money. And for what? For philosophy? I don't know.
turns.zh: 很多东西之所以算 DeFi，是因为它跑在去中心化交易所上，但其中一条腿是 USDC 或 USDT，对吧？那就是中心化稳定币。我只是觉得，如果朝鲜黑客能把全部钱都拿走，Binance 的处境会糟糕得多。为了什么？为了理念？我不知道。

turns.en: Existential purpose seems important.
turns.zh: 存在的意义似乎挺重要的。

turns.en: Oh, I disagree. I don't think the existential purpose of Binance is to support permissionless, irreversible transactions. I don't think anyone anywhere near Binance cares at all about that. I think the purpose of Binance is to enable financial transactions and It would be stupid to have the financial transactions all end up in the pockets of North Korea.
turns.zh: 哦，我不同意。我不认为 Binance 的存在意义是支持无需许可、不可逆转的交易。我不觉得 Binance 附近有任何人哪怕一点点在意这件事。我认为 Binance 的目的是促成金融交易，而这些金融交易全都落进朝鲜的口袋里，那就太蠢了。

turns.en: I guess I just think about who's left in crypto these days. You got some grifters and scammers. You got some hackers. You got some willing marks. You've got some true diehard libertarians and like anti-state people.
turns.zh: 我只是会想，如今加密圈里还剩下些什么人。有一些骗子和诈骗犯，有一些黑客，有一些甘愿上钩的冤大头，还有一些真正死硬的自由意志主义者和反国家的人。

turns.en: I think everything you just said is like 1% of the market. I think that 99% of the market is like hyper liquid trading perps on SpaceX. I think it's like stateless financial speculations.
turns.zh: 我觉得你刚说的那些加起来大概占市场的 1%。我认为市场里 99% 是在 Hyperliquid 上交易 SpaceX 的永续合约（perps）。我觉得那是无国界的金融投机。

turns.en: Perps? What is this?
turns.zh: 永续合约？这是什么？

turns.en: It's people trading financial products in a crypto rails kind of way. I'm exaggerating. I say 1%. Like what you said is like 40%, but like.
turns.zh: 就是人们用加密轨道（crypto rails）的方式在交易金融产品。我在夸张，我说 1%，其实你说的那些可能占 40%，但是……

turns.en: I feel a little better.
turns.zh: 我感觉好受一点了。

turns.en: I think that like when Binance thinks about what it does, it's like, we want to like list bets on SpaceX stock. We want to list financial products. We want to like get into the financial mainstream. Like that's the game these days. Like stateless libertarianism is embarrassing.
turns.zh: 我觉得 Binance 在想自己是干什么的时候，想的是：我们想上线押注 SpaceX 股票的产品，我们想上线金融产品，我们想进入金融主流。这才是现在的玩法。无国界的自由意志主义已经挺丢人了。

turns.en: I guess, but are you answering who the Binance client is? And I was asking who is in crypto. Does that distinction not matter?
turns.zh: 我想是吧，但你回答的是「Binance 的客户是谁」，而我问的是「加密圈里有谁」。这个区别不重要吗？

turns.en: Are those different? I don't know. I just think that like the money that exists in crypto is about like financial infrastructure and crypto and like using crypto rails to trade financial products much, much, much, much more than it is about like fidelity to Satoshi Nakamoto's vision or whatever.
turns.zh: 这两个有区别吗？我不知道。我只是觉得，加密世界里存在的这些钱，其意义在于金融基础设施、在于用加密轨道交易金融产品，远远多于对 Satoshi Nakamoto 愿景之类的忠诚。

turns.en: Yeah, fair enough.
turns.zh: 是啊，说得有道理。

turns.en: Yeah. And that's why they use USDC and Tether, right? Which, by the way, like one problem with USDC and Tether is that, oh, they enable reversible transactions. The other problem is that they're indexed to the US dollar, right? Oh, I don't believe in the US dollar. I believe only hard currency like Bitcoin. No, nobody believes that anymore. It's crazy.
